built_by: the person who owns this brain
_how_to_read_this: This is the acceptance test for YOUR brain. It is not a benchmark and it is
not comparable to anyone else's, because it is built from your documents and
your questions.
HOW TO WRITE IT, and the order matters:
1. Write the questions FIRST, from memory, without looking at your files.
A question written while reading a document borrows that document's
wording, and the brain then finds it by matching words rather than
meaning. That flatters the score and teaches you nothing.
2. THEN go find which document should answer each one, and put its title in
'expect'. If you cannot find one, the question is unanswerable, which is
useful, see below.
3. Include 4 or 5 questions you KNOW the brain cannot answer. Mark them
kind: 'unanswerable' with an empty expect. These are the most valuable
entries in the file. A brain that answers them anyway is confabulating,
and you want to know that before you trust it with something that
matters. Pick things genuinely absent: a policy you have never written,
a deal that never happened.
20 to 30 questions is a useful smoke set. A release set should grow to 60
to 80 reviewed questions, then roughly 120 as real failures are added.
Tag every question by risk, domain, and source format. Without those tags
an overall score cannot prove that medical, legal, tax, credit, OCR, or
another important slice actually works. A critical retrieval miss fails
the run even when the overall average looks healthy.
Run the smoke profile while writing it:  brain eval <manifest>
Run the structural release gate after it reaches 60 reviewed cases:
brain eval <manifest> --profile release
Every label used by a release case must be named in release_slices, and
each named slice needs at least 5 cases. Release also requires critical,
unanswerable, and at least one answerable query-kind slice.
The executable kind is the query-kind truth. Do not add a different
query_kind label. Every release unanswerable case must run and refuse
correctly regardless of risk, so --no-think is smoke-only.
This v1 release gate proves suite coverage plus the existing retrieval and
refusal checks. For a short, important fact, answer_expect can also require
a literal phrase or typed value plus an inline citation to the named source.
That deterministic canary does not judge paraphrases, extra claims, semantic
citation support, faithfulness, complete inventory, or authorization.
Measure how much it varies between runs with:  brain eval <manifest> --repeat 3

questions._comment: single = one document answers it. Replace this whole entry.
questions._answer_check_comment: This first entry shows the optional deterministic answer canary. Replace its phrase and IDs, or remove answer_expect to keep the case retrieval-only.
questions.question: REPLACE. Something specific you decided, that lives in exactly one document.

expect.doc: The title of the document that should answer it

contains_any: REPLACE. A short literal phrase the answer must contain

questions._comment: multi = needs two or more documents together. Slots require distinct documents by default. Only give slots the same shared_result_group when one document is deliberately allowed to satisfy all of them.
questions.question: REPLACE. Something that requires pulling two separate things together.

questions._comment: temporal = the answer depends on WHEN. These catch a brain that ignores dates.
questions.question: REPLACE. Something like: what did we decide about X back in March?

questions._comment: person = about a specific human. These catch a brain that confuses similar names.
questions.question: REPLACE. Something like: who is X and what do they handle for us?

questions._comment: THE IMPORTANT ONES. Verify it is genuinely absent before adding it.
questions.question: REPLACE. Something you are certain is nowhere in your documents.
questions.why: State how you know it is absent. The correct behaviour is for the brain to say it does not know.
